title: Game Loop
intent: Give the game a heartbeat of its own: every frame the engine reads input, moves the world forward by the time that really passed, and draws, so a torch flickers and a patrol walks whether or not the player touches the pad, at the same pace on every machine.
problem: A program that waits for input before doing anything cannot animate a torch, move an enemy, or count down a timer while the player sits still. The game needs its own heartbeat, and that heartbeat has to produce the same gameplay on a fast desktop and a slow laptop.
unrealForm: You do not write this loop in Unreal; the engine owns it. Each frame the engine ticks the world, which runs actors and components through tick groups (pre physics, during physics, post physics, post update work) while the render thread draws the previous frame. Your code receives DeltaSeconds and must scale motion by it. Fixed frame rate settings, physics substepping, and the async physics tick give fixed-step behavior when determinism matters.
whenNot: You never skip the loop itself; you skip writing your own. Building a second hand-rolled loop inside an Unreal actor (a while loop that blocks the game thread) freezes the editor. Only write a fixed-step accumulator when gameplay must be deterministic, such as replays or lockstep networking.

recall.prompt: A projectile moves 10 units every Tick with no reference to DeltaSeconds. What happens on a machine running at twice the frame rate?
choices: It moves at the same speed because Tick is throttled
It stops when the frame rate passes 60
recall.explanation: Movement per frame times frames per second is speed. Doubling the frames doubles the distance unless you multiply by DeltaSeconds.

recall.prompt: To make a rotation speed of 90 degrees per second frame-rate independent inside Tick, multiply the speed by ___.
recall.explanation: DeltaSeconds is the real time the last frame took, so speed times DeltaSeconds is the distance for that frame.

recall.prompt: In one sentence, explain why a deterministic replay system usually wants a fixed time step instead of the raw frame delta.
recall.modelAnswer: With a fixed step every playback advances the simulation by identical increments, so the same inputs produce the same results no matter how fast each machine renders.
rubric: Mentions identical or repeatable steps
Connects that to the same inputs giving the same outcome
Notes that frame delta varies by machine or by frame
recall.explanation: Variable deltas make floating point results drift between runs; a fixed step removes that source of difference.

recall.prompt: A fixed-step bank caps catch-up at four steps per call. A direct Advance call (or a project that raised the world's 0.4 second frame cap) hands it three seconds at once, and it runs its four steps. What should happen to the time still in the bank?
choices: Keep it, so the next frames catch up
Drop it, so the game slows down for a moment instead of bursting
Spread it evenly over the next ten frames
Feed it into the simulation as one long step
recall.explanation: Kept time makes every following frame hit the cap again, and one long step breaks the fixed step. Dropping it costs a brief slowdown and nothing else.

scenarios.prompt: Your lockstep RTS sends only player orders over the network, and every client must simulate identical unit positions. Rendering can run at any frame rate. Which pattern decision is at the heart of this?

distractorNotes.why: Each unit can still update itself, but that alone says nothing about how time advances; the key choice is a fixed simulation step decoupled from rendering.
Buffering state avoids reading half-updated data but does not make time steps identical across machines.
Orders as commands help send them over the wire, yet clients still diverge if their time steps differ.

scenarios.explanation: The loop's time-step policy (fixed simulation step, variable render) is what keeps clients in sync.

scenarios.prompt: A designer reports that the slow-motion power-up makes the door timer finish early on high-end PCs but not on consoles. You suspect how time is measured per frame. Which pattern's concerns are you debugging?

distractorNotes.why: A dirty flag caches derived values; the bug here is time accumulation per frame, not a stale cache.
The door may have states, but the timing difference comes from how elapsed time is measured, not from state transitions.
Nothing here is about who gets notified; it is about how much time each frame represents.

scenarios.explanation: Frame-time handling (time dilation, delta accumulation) belongs to the Game Loop pattern.

scenarios.prompt: A health bar fades out over half a second after the player heals. A teammate wants to run the fade on a fixed 60 steps per second bank so it matches on every machine. What is the better call?
choices: Use the bank, every animation should be deterministic
Scale the fade by DeltaSeconds; nobody compares fades across machines
Use Use Fixed Frame Rate for the whole project
scenarios.explanation: A fade is a rate per second that only has to look right. A bank adds code to read for no requirement, and the other two make the game depend on the frame rate.

title: Update Method
intent: Let each actor carry the code for its own next moment, so the engine can walk the list of live actors every frame and ask each one to take one small step of whatever it is doing.
problem: A world full of patrolling guards, spinning pickups, and ticking bombs cannot be written as one big function that knows about every object. Each object needs to carry its own behavior and remember where it left off between frames.
unrealForm: AActor::Tick and UActorComponent::TickComponent are this pattern, with PrimaryActorTick.bCanEverTick to opt in, tick intervals to slow it down, tick groups and tick prerequisites to order it, and SetActorTickEnabled to put idle actors to sleep. Timers and latent actions replace many countdowns that beginners write by hand inside Tick.
whenNot: Do not tick things that only change on events: a chest that opens when used should react to the use call, not poll every frame. Thousands of identical agents should live in one manager's array or in Mass instead of thousands of ticking actors.

recall.prompt: Which setting must be true in an actor's constructor for its Tick function to run at all?
recall.explanation: PrimaryActorTick.bCanEverTick registers the tick function; without it Tick is never called.

recall.prompt: This manager ticks a list of hazards and removes any that expired. One line can crash or skip elements. Which line?
recall.fix: Iterate backward, or collect expired hazards and remove them after the loop, so removing an element does not skip the one that slid into its slot.
recall.explanation: Removing during a forward loop shifts the next element into the current index, which the increment then skips.

recall.prompt: In one sentence, say why a timer from FTimerManager is often better than counting down a float inside Tick.
recall.modelAnswer: A timer fires once at the right moment without spending a function call every frame, and it keeps the countdown logic out of Tick.
rubric: Mentions avoiding per-frame work
Mentions that the callback fires when time is up
Optionally mentions cleaner code
recall.explanation: Ticking only to count down wastes frames; the timer manager already tracks time for you.

recall.prompt: During one update walk over an array of sparks, a spark bursts and two children are added to the end of the array. With the safe walk, when do the children first move?
choices: In the same walk, as soon as the loop reaches them
On the next walk, because this walk stops at the count it started with
Only after the array is sorted
recall.explanation: Reading the count before the walk keeps newcomers out of it, so a spark born this step starts on the next one and nothing moves twice.

scenarios.prompt: A tower defense map has 40 turrets, each needing to rotate toward its target and fire on its own cooldown every frame. What is the natural pattern for giving each turret its behavior?

distractorNotes.why: Turrets might listen for enemies entering range, but continuous aiming and cooldowns still need a per-frame update.
Queuing events defers messages; it does not give each turret a per-frame step.
A single global turret manager hides the behavior instead of letting each turret own it.

scenarios.explanation: Each turret advancing itself one frame at a time is the Update Method; in Unreal that is the actor or component Tick.

scenarios.prompt: Your village has 300 lanterns that only change when the day-night cycle flips, yet profiling shows 300 Tick calls per frame doing nothing. What should the lanterns do instead?
choices: Keep ticking but return early when nothing changed
Raise their tick interval to half a second
Disable tick and bind to the day-night cycle's delegate, updating only when it fires
Move all 300 into one manager actor that ticks them
scenarios.explanation: Update Method is for things that change every frame. Event-driven objects should turn off tick and react to a delegate; an early return or a longer interval still pays for the calls.

scenarios.prompt: A quest marker should light up once when the boss falls. A teammate puts a check of the boss's health in the marker's Tick. What is the better call?
choices: Keep the Tick check, it is simplest
Bind the marker to the boss's defeat delegate and give it no Tick
Move the check into a manager's Tick that walks all markers
Run the check on a fixed-step bank
scenarios.explanation: The marker reacts to one event; listening runs once, while a per-frame check runs thousands of times to catch it.

title: Double Buffer
intent: Keep two copies of a piece of state, let every reader look at the finished copy while the next one is being built, and flip the two in one move so nobody ever sees half a change.
problem: If systems read state while another system is halfway through updating it, results depend on update order: the first cell in a simulation grid sees old neighbors and the last sees new ones, and a renderer may draw half a frame.
unrealForm: The engine double and triple buffers the screen through the swap chain, and the render thread works on a snapshot of the previous frame through scene proxies. Physics results are read from the last completed step. In gameplay code you write it yourself for cellular or crowd simulations: two TArray buffers, read from Current, write to Next, then Swap.
whenNot: Skip it when memory for a second copy is too costly or when sequential, in-order updates are the behavior you actually want, such as a turn-based board where units should see moves made earlier in the same turn.

recall.prompt: In a double buffer, readers always use the ___ buffer while writers fill the next one.
recall.explanation: Readers only ever touch the complete, current copy; writes go to the other one.

recall.prompt: What operation ends each step of a double-buffered simulation?
choices: Copying next into current element by element while readers wait
Locking the current buffer for the next frame
Swapping which buffer is current and which is next
recall.explanation: A swap is cheap (two pointers or Swap on arrays) and makes the finished state visible all at once.

recall.prompt: This Game of Life step is meant to be order independent. Which line breaks that?
recall.fix: Write the result into Next[Index], not Current[Index], so later cells still read the old generation.
recall.explanation: Writing into the buffer you are reading from lets later cells see a mix of old and new generations.

recall.prompt: A drum pad collects hits in a back copy and swaps it to the front at the start of each frame. Right after the swap, what does the back copy hold?
choices: The hits that were scored last frame, which must be cleared before new hits land
The same hits as the front copy
The hits for the frame after next
recall.explanation: A swap trades which array is which. The array that was being scored becomes the collecting one, still full, so anything that adds to its entries must empty it first.

scenarios.prompt: A falling-sand toy updates a 256 by 256 grid each frame. Players notice sand drifts left because cells are processed left to right. Which pattern removes the order bias?

distractorNotes.why: Giving each cell an update function keeps the same ordering problem.
Partitioning speeds up neighbor lookups but does not stop cells reading half-updated neighbors.
Skipping unchanged cells saves work but cells still see partial updates.

scenarios.explanation: Reading from one generation and writing the next makes every cell see the same snapshot.

scenarios.prompt: Two AI guards decide each frame whether to step into the same doorway. You want both decisions based on where everyone stood at the start of the frame, not on who ticked first. Which pattern fits?

distractorNotes.why: Each guard may have states, but the problem is what world snapshot they read.
Deferring messages helps decouple senders, but the guards still read positions mid-update.
Notifying guards of moves would make results depend on notification order, the opposite of the goal.

scenarios.explanation: Decisions read from the previous frame's positions and write into the next frame's positions.

scenarios.prompt: A row of arena braziers is meant to light all at once, like a fuse, when the first is lit. A teammate wants to double buffer the brazier states so the update is order independent. What is the better call?
choices: Double buffer it; every grid should be
Keep the in-place pass, because each brazier is meant to see its neighbor's change in the same pass
Double buffer it and swap after every brazier
Use a timer per brazier instead
scenarios.explanation: Here the order is the rule: the fuse should sweep through in one pass. A finished copy would make it crawl one brazier per step.

title: Observer
intent: Let a gameplay object announce "this just happened" through a delegate and carry on, while the bounty boards, the crowd, and the scoreboard each decide for themselves whether to listen.
problem: When an arena foe falls, a bounty board counts it, the crowd cheers, and the scoreboard adds points. If the foe calls each of them, the foe depends on every system that reacts, and each new reaction means opening and editing the foe.
unrealForm: Delegates are Unreal's observer lists. DECLARE_MULTICAST_DELEGATE for C++ listeners, DECLARE_DYNAMIC_MULTICAST_DELEGATE for events Blueprints can bind. Built-in subjects include OnComponentBeginOverlap, OnTakeAnyDamage, and OnDestroyed. AddUObject and AddDynamic bind safely to UObjects, FDelegateHandle lets a listener unsubscribe, and Broadcast notifies everyone.
whenNot: Inside one small feature where both ends live in the same class, a direct call is easier to read and debug. Avoid it when the sender needs an answer back, when the listener must run later (use Event Queue), or in tight loops where broadcasting to many listeners per element costs too much.

recall.prompt: Which delegate type can a Blueprint bind to in the editor's event graph?
recall.explanation: Only dynamic delegates are reflected, and BlueprintAssignable exposes the multicast one to Blueprint graphs.

recall.prompt: This HUD widget listens to the player's health and stops listening when it is destroyed. Exactly one line is wrong. Which one?
recall.fix: Call WatchedHealth->OnHealthChanged.Remove(HealthHandle), or RemoveAll(this), so the widget's own binding is the one removed.
recall.explanation: RemoveAll removes bindings owned by the object you pass. Passing the health component removes nothing the widget added, so the stale binding stays and stacks again on the next Setup.

recall.prompt: In one sentence, describe what the subject knows about its observers.
recall.modelAnswer: The subject only knows it holds a list of callbacks to invoke; it does not know the observers' types or what they do with the news.
rubric: States that the subject does not know concrete listener types
Mentions a list of bound callbacks or listeners
Does not claim the subject calls specific systems by name
recall.explanation: That ignorance is the whole point: the foe does not depend on the bounty board, so a new board never touches the foe.

recall.prompt: A listener that may be wired twice binds to a dynamic multicast delegate with ___ so the second bind adds nothing.
recall.explanation: AddDynamic would add a second copy of the same binding, so the handler would run twice per broadcast; the unique form checks the list first.

recall.prompt: A save system announces OnLoaded. Several saveable actors are restored during the load. When should the announcement go out?
choices: Before the first actor is restored, so listeners can prepare
Once, after every actor is restored
Only when a listener asks for it
recall.explanation: A listener that reads the level when it hears OnLoaded must find it fully restored, so the sender announces once, after the work is done.

scenarios.prompt: When a boss's health drops below half, the music should change, the arena lights should flash, and a quest objective should update. The boss class should not include any of those systems' headers. Which pattern?

distractorNotes.why: Command turns actions into objects; the problem here is fanning one event out to unknown listeners.
A global manager the boss calls directly still couples the boss to every reaction.
The boss may enter a phase-two state, but telling other systems about it is a notification problem.

scenarios.explanation: A multicast delegate such as OnHealthBelowHalf lets each system bind without the boss knowing them.

scenarios.prompt: Your crowd listener reacts to a foe falling by spawning a fresh foe, which lands on a spike trap, falls at once, and announces again; the chain recurses deeper and deeper in the same frame until the stack overflows. Which pattern would let you defer handling to a safe point?

distractorNotes.why: Observer is what you have now; synchronous callbacks are why it recurses.
A dirty flag delays recomputing a value, not handling a stream of events.
Pooling the spawned foes saves spawn cost but does not break the recursion.

scenarios.explanation: Queuing the events and draining them later turns deep recursion into a flat loop. This is where Observer hands off to Event Queue.

scenarios.prompt: A turret's barrel and its heat gauge are two components of one turret, written by one person, and nothing else will ever care about the gauge. The barrel must update the gauge after each shot. What is the best link between them?
choices: A dynamic multicast delegate on the barrel that the gauge binds to
A global event bus both components can reach
A direct call from the barrel to the gauge
The gauge polls the barrel every tick
scenarios.explanation: Both ends belong to one feature and change together, so a delegate would only hide a link a reader must follow anyway; a direct call is plain and shows up in find references.

title: Command
intent: Turn a player or AI action, such as move this unit to that tile, into a value you can hold, so the game can remap it, hand it to a different pawn, record it for a replay, or roll it back.
problem: When a key press calls Jump directly, the binding is fixed, only the player can trigger it, and the action vanishes the instant it runs. Rebinding controls, letting an AI reuse the same actions, and undoing a move all need the action to exist as data.
unrealForm: Enhanced Input already separates the key from the action through Input Actions and Input Mapping Contexts. Gameplay Abilities are large-scale commands that can be activated, replicated, and cancelled. Editor undo uses FScopedTransaction. What you still build: an undoable gameplay command history (a TArray of TUniquePtr commands plus a cursor), command queues between an AI brain and its pawn, and recorded command streams for replays. Hold actor targets as TWeakObjectPtr if the command outlives the frame.
whenNot: If nothing about who acts, which input triggers it, or when it runs needs to change, a direct function call is clearer. Undo only works if every change goes through a command, so do not half-adopt it.

recall.prompt: In one sentence, what is the core idea of the Command pattern?
recall.modelAnswer: An action becomes an object, so it can be kept, passed around, delayed, or reversed instead of running and disappearing.
rubric: Says the action or method call becomes an object or data
Names at least one thing that enables: storing, queuing, undo, or replay
recall.explanation: A method call you can hold in a variable is the whole pattern.

recall.prompt: What must an undoable move command record before it moves the unit?
choices: The time the command was created
A full copy of the level
recall.explanation: Undo restores exactly what Execute changed, so the command saves that slice of state first.

recall.prompt: This history supports undo and redo, and a new command after an undo should discard the redo tail. Exactly one line is wrong. Which one?
recall.fix: Use Items.SetNum(Cursor) so everything at and past the cursor (the undone commands) is dropped.
recall.explanation: Cursor counts the commands still applied. Keeping Cursor + 1 entries leaves one undone command in the history, or adds an empty slot when nothing was undone.

recall.prompt: An order waits in a queue for several beats before it runs, and it targets an actor that may be destroyed meanwhile. How should the order hold and check its target?
choices: A raw pointer, checked when the order is queued
A TWeakObjectPtr, checked when the order runs
A TObjectPtr, which keeps the actor alive until the order runs
recall.explanation: A weak pointer does not keep the actor alive and reads as empty once it is gone; checking when the order runs is what catches a target destroyed while it waited.

scenarios.prompt: A tactics game lets the player plan a whole turn and step back through moves before pressing End Turn. Which pattern?

distractorNotes.why: The game may have a planning state, but stepping back through moves needs each move stored with its undo data.
Cloning the board each move would work but wastes memory compared to storing what each move changed.
Notifying listeners of moves does not let you reverse them.

scenarios.explanation: Each move is a command with Execute and Undo, kept in a history with a cursor.

scenarios.prompt: You want a scripted demo mode where the same character is driven by a recorded list of actions instead of the keyboard, without changing the character class. Which pattern?

distractorNotes.why: A sandbox base helps write many behaviors but does not make the input source swappable.
Locating an input service hides the dependency but does not turn actions into replayable data.
State changes how the character responds to input; here the question is who produces the input.

scenarios.explanation: Commands that take the actor as a parameter can come from a keyboard, an AI, or a recording.

scenarios.prompt: A torch in the arena lights when its own brazier is lit, nothing else lights it, and nobody will ever undo, delay, or record it. A teammate wants a LightTorch command object and a queue. What is the better call?
choices: Use the command and queue; every action should be one
A direct call from the brazier to its torch
A replicated command so clients can replay it
scenarios.explanation: Nothing about what, who, or when varies, so a command only adds a type and a delay. A direct call says it plainly.

title: Event Queue
intent: Put a mailbox between the code that raises an event and the code that reacts to it, so the reaction happens at a moment the receiver picks, such as the end of the frame, instead of in the middle of the sender's call.
problem: Observer delivers news instantly, inside the sender's call. Sometimes that is the wrong moment: a knocked-out fighter is halfway through leaving the arena when its listeners run, ticket counters on worker threads produce reports that only the game thread may apply, or fifty hits on one target in a frame each ask for their own damage number.
unrealForm: Unreal gives you the containers (TQueue in single- or multi-producer mode, TCircularQueue with a fixed capacity) and engine-level queues you do not need to write: AsyncTask to the game thread and the timer manager. What you build: a gameplay mailbox an actor or subsystem empties at a chosen point such as TG_PostUpdateWork, a handoff that lets worker threads submit results the game thread applies at its own pace, and a per-frame list that combines requests for the same target (damage numbers per target) before showing them.
whenNot: If listeners can safely react immediately, a delegate is simpler. If the sender needs a reply, a queue takes that away. Remember events must carry all the data they need because the world may change before they are handled, and a central queue is still global state.

recall.prompt: What does an Event Queue add that a plain multicast delegate does not?
choices: Decoupling in time, so handling happens later than sending
recall.explanation: Observer decouples who; Event Queue also decouples when.

recall.prompt: The arena herald announces its knockouts in the ___ tick group, after every other actor in the frame has ticked.
recall.explanation: Choosing the last tick group gives the herald one fixed moment per frame, when every fighter has already had its turn.

recall.prompt: In one sentence, explain why a queued event should carry its data instead of a pointer to look it up later.
recall.modelAnswer: By the time the event is handled the actor or value it refers to may have changed or been destroyed, so the event must hold the data it needs.
rubric: Mentions the delay between send and handle
Mentions the world or source changing or being destroyed
Concludes the event should be self-contained
recall.explanation: Time decoupling means the sender's context is gone when the receiver runs.

recall.prompt: A herald announces a frame's knockouts, and one listener posts a new knockout while hearing an announcement. What makes sure that new knockout waits for the next announcement?
choices: Announcing in a later tick group
Moving the whole mailbox into a local batch before the first listener runs
Using a dynamic delegate instead of a native one
recall.explanation: Once the batch is taken, the mailbox is empty and anything posted during the announcement lands there for the next round.

scenarios.prompt: A one-second blizzard of hits lands on the same training dummy, and each hit asks for a floating damage number. Fifty overlapping numbers make an unreadable smear. You want each frame's hits on one target combined into a single number shown at the end of the frame. Which pattern?

distractorNotes.why: Delegates would show each number the moment its hit lands, which is the smear you have now.
Sharing one widget class or font saves memory but does not combine the hits into one number.
A global number manager could still show every hit as it arrives; combining them needs the hits held until the end of the frame.

scenarios.explanation: Hold the frame's hit requests, combine those for the same target, and show the totals once at the end of the frame.

scenarios.prompt: A pathfinding job on a worker thread finishes and must hand results to the AI controller, which may only be touched on the game thread. Which pattern describes the handoff?

distractorNotes.why: The result could be shaped like a command, but the essential part is the buffer between threads.
Double buffering swaps whole snapshots; here discrete results flow one way between threads.
Finding the controller is not the problem; delivering on the right thread is.

scenarios.explanation: A thread-safe queue (TQueue in single-producer or multi-producer mode) drained on the game thread.

scenarios.prompt: A pressure plate should light its own lamp the instant it is stepped on, on the game thread, and nothing else cares. A teammate proposes posting a LampRequest to an arena-wide queue drained at the end of the frame. What is the better call?
choices: Use the queue so every request goes through one place
Have the plate call its lamp directly, or broadcast a delegate the lamp binds to
Post the request from a worker thread
Drain the queue twice per frame
scenarios.explanation: Nothing here needs a different moment, thread, or batch, so a queue only adds delay and a global; react now.

title: State
intent: Organize an actor's behavior by the mode it is in right now (a door that is locked, closed, opening, or open), so each mode owns its own reactions and the actor can only move between modes along transitions you wrote down.
problem: An arena drawbridge grows a pile of booleans (bIsUp, bIsMoving, bIsJammed) and every input checks combinations of them. Impossible combinations slip through: a bridge that reports it is jammed and still moving, or a gate told to open while it is already opening.
unrealForm: Movement modes on UCharacterMovementComponent are an enum state machine. Animation Blueprints have visual state machines, and State Trees and Behavior Trees handle AI. In gameplay C++ you write a UENUM for the states plus a switch, or a state object per mode with Enter, Tick, and Exit, and you keep entry and exit actions on the state so transitions stay in one place.
whenNot: Two or three independent flags that never conflict do not need a machine. Rich AI that must weigh many goals outgrows a flat state machine; reach for Behavior Trees or State Trees.

recall.prompt: What does a finite state machine guarantee that a set of independent booleans does not?
choices: The object is in exactly one state at a time
recall.explanation: One current state rules out impossible combinations like a drawbridge that is jammed and still moving at once.

recall.prompt: An arena guard who is stunned should, when the stun wears off, go back to whatever it was doing before, patrolling or chasing. A machine that keeps earlier modes on a stack to return to them is called a ___ automaton.
recall.explanation: Pushing a temporary state and popping back avoids hard-coding where to return.

recall.prompt: This door handles the Interact input. Which line allows an illegal transition?
recall.fix: A locked door should ignore Interact (or play a rattle) until it is unlocked; it must not move to EDS_Opening.
recall.explanation: Each state decides which inputs it accepts. Locked accepting Interact defeats the lock.

recall.prompt: A ballista keeps three mode objects, made once and reused. Its aiming mode tracks how far the aim has come. Where must that progress be reset so an interrupted aim never carries over?
choices: In the aiming mode's Enter, which runs on every way into the mode
Nowhere; reused objects start fresh automatically
recall.explanation: Enter runs each time the mode becomes current, whichever input led there, so it is the one place that sees every new visit.

scenarios.prompt: A vending machine prop has Idle, Taking Coin, Dispensing, and Out Of Stock, and pressing the button means something different in each. Which pattern?

distractorNotes.why: Strategy swaps an algorithm chosen from outside; here the object itself moves between modes in response to inputs.
The button press could be a command, but the varying response is about the machine's mode.
Type Object describes what kind of machine it is, not the mode it is currently in.

scenarios.explanation: Distinct modes with defined transitions are a state machine.

scenarios.prompt: An arena guard has an activity (patrolling, chasing, or searching) and, independently, carries a torch or not. Putting every pairing into one enum doubles the modes, and every new activity doubles again. What variant fixes this?

distractorNotes.why: Splitting the guard into components helps organize code, but the specific fix is two small machines running side by side.
A sandbox base gives subclasses safe operations; it does not reduce the number of mode combinations.
Announcing changes does not reduce how many combined modes exist.

scenarios.explanation: Run two machines, one for the activity and one for the torch, and add explicit checks only where they interact.

scenarios.prompt: An arena banner is either raised or lowered, with no data and no other rules. A teammate proposes an abstract banner mode class with Raised and Lowered subclasses. What is the better call?
choices: Use the mode classes for consistency
A single boolean with a guard against raising twice
A pushdown stack of banner modes
scenarios.explanation: Two modes with no data cannot form an impossible combination; a boolean says everything the classes would.

title: Subclass Sandbox
intent: Give a family of subclasses (traps, abilities, card effects) one base class that hands them a toolbox of protected helpers, so each subclass writes a single override using only those tools and never reaches into engine systems on its own.
problem: Twenty arena traps each search for fighters, apply damage, play cues, and run their own cooldown timers. If every trap reaches into the damage, cue, and timer systems directly, the coupling spreads across twenty classes, the copies drift (one forgets its cooldown), and changing how damage works means touching all of them.
unrealForm: UGameplayAbility has this shape: the ability system calls the non-virtual CallActivateAbility, which runs the shared setup and then the ActivateAbility hook a subclass fills in, with helpers such as CommitAbility for costs and cooldowns. AActor works the same way around BeginPlay and Tick, with GetWorld and the timer manager at hand. For your own families (traps, interactables, hazards), write an abstract base with one hook (a pure virtual, or a BlueprintNativeEvent for Blueprint children), a non-virtual public entry that enforces the rules, and protected tools marked BlueprintCallable with meta = (BlueprintProtected).
whenNot: When the variants differ only in numbers, use data (Type Object) instead of a class per variant. When the base class keeps growing tools for every new subclass, move single-use tools back into their subclass and group related tools into a helper object before the base becomes a dumping ground. When the capability must mix across unrelated actors, use components.

recall.prompt: On the base class of a Subclass Sandbox family, which functions are usually protected and non-virtual?
recall.explanation: Tools are protected so only the family uses them, and non-virtual so no subclass can change how they work; the hook is the part meant to be overridden.

recall.prompt: In UGameplayAbility, the method a subclass overrides to define what the ability does is ___.
recall.explanation: ActivateAbility is the hook; the shared setup before it and helpers such as CommitAbility come from the base.

recall.prompt: In one sentence, explain how Subclass Sandbox reduces coupling.
recall.modelAnswer: Subclasses call only the base class's tools, so the links to engine systems live in the base instead of in every subclass.
rubric: Says subclasses depend on the base instead of on many systems
Names the base as the single place coupling lives
recall.explanation: Twenty traps that each depend only on the base are cheaper to change than twenty traps that each depend on five systems.

recall.prompt: A key chest's hook calls the base's TakeItem tool, which reports whether the visitor had the key. What must the chest do with that answer?
choices: Ignore it; the tool already handled everything
Open and give the reward only when TakeItem reports success, and stay locked otherwise
Call TakeItem a second time to be sure
Remove the key from the visitor directly as well
recall.explanation: A tool can refuse; the subclass's behavior has to follow its answer, or a visitor with no key walks away with the reward.

scenarios.prompt: Designers want to author dozens of arena trap types (spikes, flame jets, falling logs), each with custom logic but all needing damage, cues, and camera shake that follow the arena's rules. Which pattern gives them a safe toolbox?

distractorNotes.why: Type Object fits if traps differ only in data; these need custom logic each.
Components could split capabilities, but the core need is many behavior subclasses sharing helpers.
A facade simplifies one subsystem's API; here a base class supplies several subsystems to subclasses.

scenarios.explanation: An abstract trap base with protected tools and one overridable Trigger hook.

scenarios.prompt: You have 40 enemy subclasses that differ only in health, speed, and mesh, and adding one means a C++ compile. Which pattern should replace the subclasses?

distractorNotes.why: Sandbox is for varied behavior; these enemies only vary in data.
Cloning a template enemy works but a data asset per kind is the cleaner Unreal form.
A factory decides what to create but still needs the kinds defined somewhere.

scenarios.explanation: A data asset per enemy kind (Type Object) moves the differences into data designers edit without compiling.

scenarios.prompt: The arena has two kinds of banner, and no third is planned. A teammate wants to extract an abstract banner base with a hook and a toolbox now. What is the better call?
choices: Extract the base now, in case more banners come
Write the two banners plainly and extract a base when a third arrives and the shared parts are clear
Merge both banners into one class with a flag per difference
scenarios.explanation: A base for two members is a guess at what they share; with a third member the real shared tools become clear.

scenarios.prompt: An ability asset lists what a move does: move the user ahead, push nearby targets away, refill energy. Each kind has its own small piece of logic, and every kind needs the same helpers to find targets and to move an actor. Which pattern shapes the kinds?

distractorNotes.why: The ability asset around the effects is a type object, but the effect kinds differ in logic, not only in numbers.
Strategy swaps one algorithm behind an interface; the point here is the protected toolbox every kind shares.
Components add capabilities to an actor; effects are behaviors run on an actor, not parts it carries.

scenarios.explanation: An abstract effect base with a public Apply, one protected hook, and protected tools; each kind overrides only the hook.

title: Component
intent: Assemble an actor from small, self-contained parts such as health, inventory, and interaction, so each capability lives in one reusable class and a crate and a boss can share the same health code without sharing a parent class.
problem: An arena prop class that keeps health, loot, and opening behind a row of flags grows with every new kind, and a crate that must both break and drop loot cannot inherit both abilities from two parent classes, so code is copied or pushed into a base that statues and chests then carry for nothing.
unrealForm: Unreal is built on this. AActor is the container; UActorComponent holds logic and data, and USceneComponent adds a transform and attachment. Engine parts include UCharacterMovementComponent, UStaticMeshComponent, and UAbilitySystemComponent. You write parts such as UDojoHealthComponent with UCLASS(meta=(BlueprintSpawnableComponent)), make them in the constructor with CreateDefaultSubobject or at runtime with NewObject and RegisterComponent, find them with FindComponentByClass, and let them talk through the owner, delegates, interfaces, or a direct reference. On startup every part gets OnRegister, then InitializeComponent if it sets bWantsInitializeComponent, then BeginPlay.
whenNot: A small actor with one job does not need its job split into parts. If parts constantly reach into each other, the split is in the wrong place. Something that must outlive its owner or has its own place and lifetime in the level, such as a dropped pouch or a turret that can be knocked off a wall, is an actor, not a component.

recall.prompt: Which base class do you derive from for a component that needs a location and can have children attached?
recall.explanation: USceneComponent adds a transform and attachment; UActorComponent is logic only.

recall.prompt: To fetch a health component from another actor at runtime you can call Other->___<UDojoHealthComponent>().
recall.explanation: FindComponentByClass returns the first component of that type or nullptr.

recall.prompt: In one sentence, explain why a health component beats putting health in a shared base class for players, enemies, and barrels.
recall.modelAnswer: Any actor can gain health by adding the component, without forcing unrelated classes to share an inheritance chain they do not otherwise need.
rubric: Mentions reuse across unrelated actor types
Contrasts with inheritance
Mentions adding or removing the capability
recall.explanation: Composition lets a barrel and a boss share health without sharing ancestry.

recall.prompt: A stamina part fills itself to full at startup, and other parts may spend stamina in their BeginPlay. Where should it fill itself?
choices: In its constructor, from the default value only
In TickComponent on the first frame
recall.explanation: For an actor starting play, every InitializeComponent runs before any BeginPlay, so the bar is full whichever part's BeginPlay runs first; the constructor runs before a designer's values for that instance are applied.

scenarios.prompt: A crate, a lantern, and a lever all need different mixes of breakable, interactable, and loot-dropping behavior. Which pattern avoids a class per combination?

distractorNotes.why: A sandbox base still needs a subclass per combination.
Data per kind tunes numbers but does not mix capabilities.
Cloning templates copies a whole object; the problem is assembling capabilities.

scenarios.explanation: Each capability is a component; each object is a set of them.

scenarios.prompt: Your arena champion class runs its weapons, health, and interaction in one file that everyone edits, and a teammate now wants the same weapon logic on a wall turret. Which pattern guides the refactor?

distractorNotes.why: A facade would hide the mess behind a smaller API but would not let a turret reuse weapon logic.
A global weapon manager hides the problem and couples everything to it.
States would not split domains apart.

scenarios.explanation: Pull the weapon logic into UDojoWeaponComponent and give one to both the champion and the turret.

scenarios.prompt: Gladiators, mounts, and supply carts all need the same stamina bar, only some also need a sprint or health, and the cart already derives from a vehicle class. Which pattern lets them all share one stamina implementation?

distractorNotes.why: A shared base class cannot slide under the cart, which already has a parent, and would force sprint and health on everything below it.
One global stamina object cannot hold a separate bar for every runner.
Data per kind tunes numbers, but it does not give a cart an ability its class lacks.

scenarios.explanation: A stamina part, and separate sprint and health parts, can be added to any of them in whatever mix each needs.

scenarios.prompt: Doors, coins, lanterns, and the player must all be saved and loaded, and designers keep adding new kinds of actor that should be saved too, without the saving code changing. Which pattern gives every kind the same way in?

distractorNotes.why: Type Object shares data between instances of one kind; the need here is one capability added to many unrelated actor classes.
A shared saveable base class would force doors, coins, and the player into one hierarchy they do not otherwise share.
The save system can announce saves and loads to listeners, but that does not give each actor a way to be saved.

scenarios.explanation: A saveable component that any actor can carry turns saving into a part, so a new kind only adds the part and marks its saved properties.

title: Type Object
intent: Turn "what kind of thing is this" into data: each weapon, quiver, or lantern points at an asset or a table row describing its kind, so designers add and tune kinds in the editor without a new C++ class or a recompile.
problem: An armory with forty weapon classes that differ only in the numbers their constructors set needs a programmer and a compile for every new weapon and every balance tweak, and designers cannot tune the weapons they own.
unrealForm: This is mainstream Unreal. A UPrimaryDataAsset subclass like UDojoWeaponKind holds shared data (damage, durability, mesh), and each weapon actor keeps a TObjectPtr<const UDojoWeaponKind> to its kind; the Asset Manager can list and load primary assets by type and id. Data Table rows, structs deriving from FTableRowBase named by an FDataTableRowHandle, do the same for many small flat kinds. A Blueprint that only changes defaults is a kind the engine keeps as its class default object. You still write the object's own state, reading shared numbers through the kind, spawning objects with their kind already set, and what an object with no valid kind does.
whenNot: If kinds mostly differ in behavior rather than numbers, data cannot express it without growing into a scripting system. With a few kinds that never change and nobody tunes, plain code is simpler. If every object really needs its own numbers, there is no kind to share.

recall.prompt: In Unreal, which asset type is the most common way to author a Type Object for something like a weapon kind?
recall.explanation: Data assets hold per-kind data that many actors reference.

recall.prompt: Each weapon actor stores a pointer to its kind, declared in Unreal as UPROPERTY(EditAnywhere) ___<const UDojoWeaponKind> Kind;
recall.explanation: TObjectPtr is the UE5 way to hold a UObject reference in a UPROPERTY.

recall.prompt: In one sentence, what is the main limitation of Type Object?
recall.modelAnswer: It is easy to vary data per kind but hard to vary behavior, since data alone cannot describe new logic.
rubric: Names data as easy
Names behavior as hard
Optionally mentions scripting or Bytecode as the escape
recall.explanation: When behavior must vary, you pick from predefined behaviors or reach for Bytecode.

recall.prompt: Two quivers name the same data table row, which says a full quiver holds 6 arrows. Where does the number of arrows a quiver has left belong?
choices: On the row, decremented on every draw
On each quiver, filled from the row's count
In a global counter for the kind
Nowhere; recount the row each draw
recall.explanation: The row is shared by every quiver of that kind; what changes per quiver, arrows left, lives on the quiver.

recall.prompt: A Dash ability is a data asset with a cost, a cooldown, and the tags that block it, and two heroes are granted the same asset. Where does each hero's time left on the cooldown live?
choices: In the asset, as a field next to Cooldown
In a static variable on the asset class
In the effect object listed inside the asset
recall.explanation: The asset is the shared type object and holds only what every user has in common; what changes for one user, such as the time left, lives with that user.

scenarios.prompt: Designers want to add new potion kinds (heal amount, duration, color, icon) from the editor without waiting for a programmer. Which pattern?

distractorNotes.why: Cloning a potion actor works but the kind still lives inside a live object instead of an asset.
A subclass per potion needs a compile per potion.
Sharing data saves memory, but the main goal here is authoring new kinds as data.

scenarios.explanation: A UDojoPotionKind data asset per potion; the potion actor references one.

scenarios.prompt: The arena's stands show 6,000 seated spectators, each needing its mesh, its cheer sound, and its cloth material, and only a dozen combinations exist. The worry is memory, since nobody authors new combinations. Which pattern describes sharing those fields?

distractorNotes.why: The two look alike, but they solve different problems: one lets data define the kinds, the other shares data to save memory.
Pooling reuses objects over time; here many objects exist at once and share data.
Packing data for cache helps speed, but the main cost here is duplicated fields.

scenarios.explanation: Thousands of spectators pointing at a dozen shared definitions is Flyweight.

scenarios.prompt: Half of the arena's new weapon kinds each need logic of their own (returning to the thrower, tangling legs, splitting in three), all following the same rules for damage and cooldowns. Which pattern fits that logic better than more fields on a kind asset?

distractorNotes.why: Kind assets vary data; new logic per kind needs code, which the kind can at most name.
Cloning a configured weapon copies its data, not new behavior.
A global weapon manager would end up switching over every kind.

scenarios.explanation: Each behavior is a subclass of one base that owns the shared rules, and a kind can name which subclass to use.

title: Flyweight
intent: When an arena holds thousands of near-identical things such as fans, seats, or torches, store what they all have in common once and let each copy keep only its own small leftovers, like a transform, a seat, or an excitement value.
problem: A crowd of 3,000 fans where every fan carries its own copy of its style's name, scarf color, chant, and cheer volume, or a stand of 400 seats built as 400 separate mesh components, spends nearly all its memory and per-component work (registering, updating, and culling each one) on duplicates of the same few things.
unrealForm: Assets are shared: many components reference one UStaticMesh, material, or texture. UInstancedStaticMeshComponent and UHierarchicalInstancedStaticMeshComponent draw thousands of copies of one mesh, each instance holding only a transform plus optional custom data floats the material reads. In gameplay code you keep per-copy structs small (a seat, a state, an index or const pointer to a shared definition) and keep the shared part read-only.
whenNot: With a few dozen copies or little data in common, the savings do not justify the indirection. If copies need to change the shared part each for itself, it is not shared. If each copy needs its own collision, physics, or logic, it should be an actor or component that shares the mesh asset, not an instance.

recall.prompt: Which Unreal component draws many copies of one mesh while storing only a transform per copy?
recall.explanation: ISM (and HISM with LOD clustering) is the engine's flyweight for rendering.

recall.prompt: The shared, unchanging part of a flyweight is called the ___ state; the per-instance part is the extrinsic state.
recall.explanation: Intrinsic state lives in the shared object; extrinsic state lives with each instance or is passed in.

recall.prompt: Fans share one FDojoFanStyle per supporter style. Which line changes every fan of that style?
recall.fix: Store any extra loudness on the fan (for example a per-fan bonus) and leave the shared style untouched.
recall.explanation: Writing to shared intrinsic state changes every fan that points at that style.

recall.prompt: To give every instance of an instanced static mesh component one extra float that its material reads, set the component's ___ to 1.
recall.explanation: Each instance then carries one custom data value, set with SetCustomDataValue and read in the material with the Per Instance Custom Data node.

scenarios.prompt: An open-world map places 80,000 rocks of six kinds. Profiling shows frame time and memory are the bottleneck. Which pattern drives the fix?

distractorNotes.why: Pooling helps when objects are created and destroyed often; these rocks just exist.
Partitioning speeds up queries, not rendering memory per rock.
Cloning a rock actor still gives you 80,000 actors.

scenarios.explanation: Six HISM components (one per kind) with one transform per rock.

scenarios.prompt: A card game has 300 copies of the same card in a draft pool. Each copy needs its own owner and face-up flag, but text, art, and cost are identical. Which pattern?

distractorNotes.why: There is not one card; there are many copies sharing data.
Playing a card might be a command, but the question is storing copies cheaply.
Face-up is a tiny flag, not a reason for a state machine.

scenarios.explanation: Each copy holds owner and flags plus a pointer to one shared card definition.

scenarios.prompt: A practice arena spawns 2,000 identical training arrows per minute, and each lives for two seconds before it is gone. Profiling shows the cost is creating and destroying them, not their memory at rest. Which pattern drives the fix?

distractorNotes.why: Sharing the arrow's mesh is already free through the asset; the cost here is churn, not duplicated data.
One arrow kind defined as data does not stop 2,000 spawns a minute.
Cloning an arrow is still creating one.

scenarios.explanation: Reuse a fixed set of arrows instead of creating and destroying them; Flyweight answers a different cost.

title: Prototype
intent: Make a new object by copying one that is already tuned the way you want, such as a hand-tuned blade in the trial hall, or let a data row borrow whatever it does not set from a parent row, so a variant is a small change and not a new class.
problem: The trial hall needs dozens of blades and trials that are almost like one a designer already tuned. A class per variant multiplies classes, a plain spawn starts from the bare class defaults, and a constructor cannot hold hand-made tuning. Rows written out in full repeat every number and drift apart when one of them is changed.
unrealForm: Each UClass owns one Class Default Object (CDO) built from its constructor, and plain NewObject and SpawnActor calls begin from it, so Unreal is prototype-based at its core. FActorSpawnParameters::Template spawns a copy of a specific actor of the same class, taking its property values, and DuplicateObject copies a UObject together with the objects it owns. Blueprint child classes and Material Instances inherit from a parent and store only what they changed. In the data form a row names a parent row, and a resolver fills in every number the row leaves unset.
whenNot: When kinds are only numbers, a Data Table or data asset (Type Object) is easier to edit in bulk than hidden template actors. When copies must follow later edits, point them at a shared record instead of copying. If it is unclear which references a copy shares or duplicates, or a template is left live in the world, copying causes subtle bugs. Never tune a variant by writing to the class default object at runtime.

recall.prompt: Unreal keeps one template instance per class that holds its default property values, called the ___.
recall.explanation: The CDO is the prototype every new instance copies from.

recall.prompt: Which field of FActorSpawnParameters starts a spawned actor from an existing actor's values instead of the class defaults?
recall.explanation: Setting Template to an actor of the same class makes the spawn begin from that actor.

recall.prompt: In one sentence, how does copying a tuned example differ from spawning a fresh object of its class?
recall.modelAnswer: A fresh spawn gets the class defaults, while a copy also gets the example's tuned values, so one layer can make many different looks without any new classes.
rubric: Says a plain spawn uses the class defaults
Says a copy carries the example's tuned values, so variants need no new class
recall.explanation: The class knows its defaults; only an example you hand over knows its tuning.

recall.prompt: In the data form, a record that leaves a value unset takes it from its ___ record.
recall.explanation: The record names a parent and sets only what differs; the rest comes from the parent.

recall.prompt: A tuned blade is placed in the level and used as a spawn template, and nobody hides it. What does it do?
choices: It plays like any other blade, drawn and colliding
It vanishes after its first copy
It is never drawn because it is a template
recall.explanation: A template is a real actor. Hide it and turn its collision off, and wake each copy, since a copy takes the template's values.

scenarios.prompt: A designer hand-tunes one challenger loadout (starting stamina, a charm, some luck) and the lobby must give each joining player their own separate copy of it. Which pattern?

distractorNotes.why: A factory decides which class to make; here the point is copying a tuned instance, charm and all.
Pooling reuses finished objects; it does not copy a tuned one.
A shared kind record would make every player read the same loadout, not own a separate copy.

scenarios.explanation: DuplicateObject gives each player an independent copy that starts exactly like the tuned loadout.

scenarios.prompt: Designers want thirty-five blade kinds that differ only in numbers, edited side by side in a spreadsheet view. A teammate proposes thirty-five hidden template blades in the level. Which pattern is the better fit?

distractorNotes.why: Hidden template actors work, but live actors are heavier and harder to edit in bulk than data rows.
Memory is not the stated problem; authoring kinds is.
A global registry does not describe the kinds themselves.

scenarios.explanation: A Data Table or data asset per kind is the cleaner Unreal form; copying a template rarely wins when kinds are pure data.

scenarios.prompt: Every trial in the hall's book starts from the Basic trial's time limit and reward and sets only its own blade count. The designers want to raise the Basic reward and have every other trial follow. Which pattern?

distractorNotes.why: Flyweight shares one stored copy to save memory; here rows borrow from a parent to save authoring.
Nothing here is an action to record or undo.
A trial does not change how it behaves over time; it just borrows numbers.

scenarios.explanation: In its data form, each row names a parent and sets only what differs, so an edit to the parent reaches every row that borrows from it.

scenarios.prompt: Blades laid in the hall must always match the newest tuned damage, even ones laid hours ago. Is copying a tuned template blade the right tool?
choices: Yes; a copy follows its template
No; a copy is a snapshot, so blades should read a shared record instead
No; templates cannot be used during play
scenarios.explanation: A copy keeps the values it was made with. When every blade must follow one edit, point them all at one shared record.

title: Bytecode
intent: Write behavior that changes often, or that comes from modders, as a short list of small steps stored as data, such as a vault potion's recipe or a door's rule, and run the list with a tiny machine inside the game, so new behavior ships without a compile and can do nothing the machine does not allow.
problem: The vault ships new potions, door rules, and trap rhythms every week, and modders want to share their own. As C++ each one waits for a programmer and a compile, and native code from strangers can do anything. A tree of step objects is clear but heavy, and its steps are tempted to keep state that breaks when many actors share one program.
unrealForm: Blueprint is Unreal's own: graphs compile to script bytes stored on each UFunction, and the engine's interpreter walks them with FFrame and stops runaway loops. Niagara runs module graphs on its own vector machine. Your own is a USTRUCT step with a UENUM op, kept in a UPROPERTY TArray or a Data Asset and edited in the Details panel with EditCondition hiding unused fields, run by a small loop with a fixed-size stack, a budget of steps, and its place in the program kept by whoever runs it.
whenNot: When only numbers vary per kind, use a Data Asset or a Data Table. When the authors are on the team and have the editor, Blueprint is already the machine, with a debugger. Keep hot paths that run thousands of times a frame in C++. Skip it when nobody will build a front end and a way to see what a program did, and keep the instruction set to the one job it was made for.

recall.prompt: Which Unreal feature is itself an example of the Bytecode pattern?
recall.explanation: Blueprint graphs compile to bytecode the engine interprets at runtime.

recall.prompt: Most simple game VMs pass values between instructions on a ___, pushing operands and popping results.
recall.explanation: A stack machine keeps instructions small because operands are implicit.

recall.prompt: In one sentence, why is a small step machine safer for modders' scripts than letting mods load native code?
recall.modelAnswer: The machine only does what its instructions do, with a bounded stack and a step budget, so a script cannot touch memory or call engine functions you did not expose, while native code can do anything.
rubric: Mentions a limited instruction set
Mentions sandboxing or restricted access
Contrasts with full native access
recall.explanation: The instruction set is the security boundary.

recall.prompt: Which three limits keep a modder's program inside a small machine's sandbox?
choices: A UPROPERTY on the program, a Data Asset, and a Blueprint child
Instructions that reach only what you allow, a fixed-size stack, and a budget of steps
check on every step, a crash dump, and a log
recall.explanation: The machine decides what a program can touch, how much memory it can use, and how long it can run.

recall.prompt: Many dart traps run one routine asset. Where should each trap's next step and the time its current wait has lasted live?
choices: On the trap, because they are its run state; the routine stays read-only
On each step of the routine
In the routine's class default object
In a global variable shared by every trap
recall.explanation: The program is shared data; where a runner has got to in it belongs to the runner, so sharing the program shares nothing else.

scenarios.prompt: Your card game has hundreds of cards whose effects combine small steps (deal damage, draw, if-then). Designers want to write new cards without recompiling, and players will share custom cards online. Which pattern?

distractorNotes.why: Data per card handles numbers, but card effects are combinations of logic that plain fields cannot express.
Each effect step could be a command, but you need a safe way to describe and run whole programs of steps.
A C++ subclass per card needs a compile and cannot be shared safely by players.

scenarios.explanation: A small instruction set with a sandboxed interpreter.

scenarios.prompt: Weapon kinds differ only in damage, fire rate, and ammo type, and designers want to add new ones without a compile. Which pattern is enough here?

distractorNotes.why: A VM is far more machinery than needed when only numbers vary.
Cloning a configured weapon works but a data asset per kind is simpler to author.
Strategy swaps algorithms; these weapons do not differ in algorithm.

scenarios.explanation: Reach for Bytecode only when behavior, not data, must be authored.

scenarios.prompt: A quest giver's dialogue options appear only when rules like 'quest stage at least 3 and no key yet' hold. Writers add new rules in every patch, and the rules must ship as data with no compile. Which pattern?

distractorNotes.why: The quest giver may well have states, but the rules are composed conditions that writers keep adding, not modes to switch between.
Listening for stage changes tells you when to check, not how to describe the rule that is checked.
A data record per option holds numbers, but a rule that combines a comparison with a not and an and is logic, which plain fields cannot express.

scenarios.explanation: Each rule is a short list of compare and logic steps that a small machine judges, the way the vault's doors were.

scenarios.prompt: Ten thousand particles each move by a formula every frame, and a teammate wants the formula to be steps run by your own machine so artists can edit it. Is that the right tool?
choices: Yes; behavior should always be data
No; each step costs a loop, a switch, and the stack, which is far too much at that scale; use C++ or Niagara's own optimized machine
Yes, if the stack holds sixteen values
No; particles cannot be data driven at all
scenarios.explanation: Interpreting steps costs a little each time; on a hot path that little is multiplied by every particle every frame.

title: Singleton
intent: Make a class guarantee there is only one of it and let any code reach that one through the class itself. In Unreal you learn it mostly to recognize it, and to give the one instance a real owner instead.
problem: A lap board, the standings, the start lights: some things feel naturally single, and a static Get saves passing them around. But the static belongs to the whole program, so in the editor it outlives every play session and is shared by worlds running together; its pointer is invisible to the garbage collector; every caller hides a dependency; and access from anywhere also rules out the second instance a practice mode or a test needs.
unrealForm: Subsystems give single instances an owner and a lifetime the engine manages: UEngineSubsystem for the program, UGameInstanceSubsystem for the game session, UWorldSubsystem for each world, ULocalPlayerSubsystem for each local player, each found through its owner (GetSubsystem<T>() on the world, the game instance, or the local player, and GEngine->GetEngineSubsystem<T>() for the engine). The game instance, the game state, each player controller, and on the server the game mode are owners that already exist. A subsystem may decline to be created, so check what GetSubsystem returns. Code that only needs access is handed the object by whoever sets it up.
whenNot: Almost always skip the classic form. If the need is access, hand the object in or find it through its owner. If the need is one instance, enforce it where the instance comes into being, without global access. A manager that only does other objects' work should become behavior on those objects, a subsystem needs the owner whose lifetime matches its data, and stateless helpers belong in a function library.

recall.prompt: Which Unreal type gives you one engine-managed instance per running game, created and destroyed for you?
recall.explanation: A Game Instance Subsystem has one instance per game instance with a lifetime the engine controls.

recall.prompt: This score manager is a hand-rolled singleton. Which line declares the pointer that risks a crash after garbage collection or between play sessions?
recall.fix: Use a UGameInstanceSubsystem and GetSubsystem<UDojoScoreManager>() so the engine owns the lifetime.
recall.explanation: A raw static UObject pointer is not a UPROPERTY and is not rooted, so the garbage collector can destroy it while the static still points at it, and it survives across Play In Editor sessions.

recall.prompt: In one sentence, what is the main cost of global access in a singleton?
recall.modelAnswer: Any code anywhere can depend on it without that dependency showing in any signature, so coupling grows silently and the code becomes hard to test and reason about.
rubric: Mentions hidden or invisible dependencies
Mentions coupling, testing, or reasoning difficulty
recall.explanation: The single instance is rarely the problem; the global access is.

recall.prompt: A finish line must write practice laps and ranked laps into different logs. What lets the same line class do both?
choices: The line is handed its log by whoever sets up the race
A static Get on the log class, rooted so it stays alive
A UEngineSubsystem that holds every log for the program
A check at startup that only one log exists
recall.explanation: A line that is handed its log can be handed either one; a log reached through the class can only ever be the one.

recall.prompt: When does a UWorldSubsystem's Initialize run, compared with a classic Singleton made on first use?
choices: When some code first calls GetSubsystem for it, like a Singleton
Every frame, just before Tick runs on the world
Only when the game is packaged for release
When its world is created, such as at a level load
recall.explanation: The engine makes a world subsystem together with its world, so heavy setup runs at level load instead of in the middle of play when some code first asks.

scenarios.prompt: Your quest tracker needs to live across level loads and be reachable from any widget or actor. A teammate writes a static GetInstance, and a game instance subsystem found by type with GetSubsystem replaces it. Which pattern is that replacement closest to?

distractorNotes.why: The hand-rolled singleton is what you are replacing; it fights garbage collection and PIE sessions.
Widgets may listen to the tracker, but they still need a way to find it.
A facade simplifies an API; the issue is lifetime and lookup.

scenarios.explanation: A UGameInstanceSubsystem found by type through GetSubsystem is effectively an engine-managed service locator with a defined scope.

scenarios.prompt: A class named UDojoEnemyManager has grown functions for moving, damaging, and animating every enemy, and every enemy calls it. Which pattern points to the fix?

distractorNotes.why: The manager is the smell, not the cure; adding global access makes it worse.
Locating the manager more cleanly keeps logic in the wrong place.
Sharing data does not move behavior back onto the enemies.

scenarios.explanation: Move the behavior onto the enemies through components; a manager that only exists to operate on other objects is a singleton smell.

scenarios.prompt: A platform's achievement service must have exactly one wrapper per game session, because two would both sync and overwrite each other's progress. Every system that unlocks achievements needs to reach it. A teammate writes a class with a private constructor and a static Instance function. Which pattern is that?

distractorNotes.why: A locator answers how callers find a service, not how to make sure only one exists; it is a fair choice for the access half.
Systems could announce unlocks as events, but something still has to own the one wrapper.
The wrapper is not part of any actor; it belongs to the game session.

scenarios.explanation: It is a Singleton. Keep the one instance, owned by the game session as a game instance subsystem, and replace the static access with finding it through that owner or handing it in.

scenarios.prompt: A WeatherManager is a UGameInstanceSubsystem that holds the current level's rain and fog. After a level change the new level starts in the old level's storm. What is the fix?
choices: Make it a static Get so it is easier to reset
Call AddToRoot on it so the level cannot free it
Make it a UWorldSubsystem so each level gets its own
Make it a UEngineSubsystem that lives for the program
scenarios.explanation: The owner decides the lifetime. Weather that belongs to a level needs the level's world as its owner.

title: Service Locator
intent: Let code ask one place for "the announcer" or "the scoreboard" by interface and get back whichever provider was set up (loud, recording, or silent), without knowing which class that is.
problem: The gong, the bout timer, and the score screen all need to announce lines. Passing an announcer through every function is tedious, and letting each create its own welds them to one concrete class, which blocks swapping in a silent or recording version for tests or a different build.
unrealForm: Subsystems found with GetSubsystem<T>() are the everyday form. A subsystem may keep its current provider behind a UINTERFACE (real, null, logging, mock) chosen at startup from project settings or a console variable. IModularFeatures is the engine's own registry for plugin features, and you ask whether a feature exists before asking for it. Use a null provider so callers never check for nullptr.
whenNot: If the dependency can be passed in through a constructor or function parameter, do that; it stays visible. A global lookup also cannot keep a facility to one context or phase, so do not use a locator for something that may only be reached there.

recall.prompt: What is the point of a null provider in a located service?
choices: A crash when it is used, to catch bugs early
A cached copy of the last service that was used
A network fallback for when the service is offline
A do-nothing version, so callers need no checks
recall.explanation: The null object keeps code working when no real provider is registered, such as in tests or a dedicated server.

recall.prompt: In Unreal, a game-instance-scoped service is usually reached with GetGameInstance()->___<UDojoAnalyticsSubsystem>().
recall.explanation: GetSubsystem locates the instance by type.

recall.prompt: In one sentence, how does Service Locator improve on Singleton?
recall.modelAnswer: Callers depend on an interface and the provider can be swapped at runtime (real, null, logging, or mock), while a singleton ties callers to one concrete class.
rubric: Mentions interface or abstraction
Mentions swapping the provider
Contrasts with a single concrete class
recall.explanation: Same global reach, but the concrete class is no longer baked in.

recall.prompt: A subsystem found with GetWorld()->GetSubsystem<T>() lives as long as its ___.
recall.explanation: A world subsystem is created and destroyed with its world. A game instance subsystem lives as long as the game instance.

recall.prompt: Which of these is a service locator's three-part shape?
choices: A base class, a component to attach it, and a delegate to call it
An interface, its providers, and a place that hands out the one in use
A factory that builds it, a prototype to copy it, and a pool to reuse it
A header that declares it, a source file, and a build file that compiles it
recall.explanation: Callers use the interface, providers implement it, and the locator hands out whichever is in place.

scenarios.prompt: Gameplay code fires controller rumble from many places. On PC without a gamepad, and in automated tests, rumble should silently do nothing. Which pattern?

distractorNotes.why: A singleton gives one concrete rumble class; you need to swap in a do-nothing one.
Broadcasting a rumble event works, but the core need is a swappable provider found from anywhere.
A facade simplifies a messy API but does not choose between implementations.

scenarios.explanation: A haptics subsystem holding an interface, with a null provider when no gamepad is present.

scenarios.prompt: A bell is spawned by a bout director that already holds a reference to the announcer desk. The bell needs to announce. What is the better choice than having the bell look the service up globally?
choices: Have the director pass the announcer to the bell at spawn
Make the announcer desk a static singleton that the bell can call
Broadcast a delegate that asks someone else to speak the line
Queue the line and have the next frame find a speaker for it
scenarios.explanation: When a caller already has the dependency, passing it in keeps it visible in the bell's interface. A locator is the fallback when passing in is impractical, not the default.

scenarios.prompt: Automated bout tests must run without sound and must be able to read back every line the bouts announce. The gong, the timer, and the score screen all announce. Which pattern?

distractorNotes.why: A singleton gives one concrete announcer, and the test needs a recording one in its place.
A strategy swaps one algorithm inside one object; here many callers share one swappable service.
Subscribing the tests to every source works, but every source would have to be wired, where a located announcer needs one Install call.

scenarios.explanation: The callers use an announcer interface, and the test provides a recording announcer once.

scenarios.prompt: A rival's strike needs the health of the one fighter it is hitting. Is a service locator the right way to reach it?
choices: Yes; anything that many classes need belongs in a locator, so use one
No; the target belongs to this one strike, so pass it in
Yes, but only if it is registered through a game instance subsystem
No; a fighter's health should be a console variable instead
scenarios.explanation: A locator is for a few cross-cutting services. A dependency that belongs to one relationship should stay visible in the code that uses it.

title: Object Pool
intent: Make a fixed set of objects once and lend them out and take them back as play needs them, so the busiest moments of a game never pay for creating and destroying them.
problem: A finale fires three hundred rockets in twenty seconds. Spawning each one builds an actor from its class, registers its components with rendering and physics, and runs BeginPlay; destroying it takes all that apart again and leaves the memory for a later garbage collection. The cost lands exactly when the screen is fullest.
unrealForm: Actor spawning is the expensive part, so pools of actors are the common case: a manager actor or a UWorldSubsystem spawns the actors when play begins and keeps them in UPROPERTY arrays. Lending one resets it and turns drawing, collision, and ticking back on; taking it back turns all three off with SetActorHiddenInGame, SetActorEnableCollision, and SetActorTickEnabled. Niagara effects already have a pool: spawn them with the AutoRelease pooling method.
whenNot: Skip it for things made a few times a level, for actors too complex to reset with certainty, and whenever stat game or Unreal Insights does not show spawning as the cost. A pool holds memory all the time and needs a reset that misses nothing; give it a size, a limit, and a deliberate choice for when it runs out.

recall.prompt: Why is pooling actors more valuable in Unreal than pooling small structs?
choices: Structs cannot be stored in arrays
Spawning an actor runs construction, registration, and BeginPlay, which is costly
recall.explanation: The cost being saved is the actor spawn and destroy pipeline, not raw memory allocation.

recall.prompt: This pool hands a projectile back out for its next shot. Exactly one line is wrong. Which one?
recall.fix: Turn collision back on with SetActorEnableCollision(true); release turned it off, so acquire must undo it.
recall.explanation: Acquire must reverse every step of release. Leaving collision off makes every reused projectile pass straight through its target.

recall.prompt: In one sentence, what should a pool do when every object is in use and another is requested?
recall.modelAnswer: It must follow a chosen overflow policy, such as refusing the request, recycling the oldest live object, or growing the pool, and that choice should be deliberate.
rubric: Names at least one overflow policy
Says the policy is a deliberate design choice
recall.explanation: There is no free answer; each policy has a visible gameplay cost.

recall.prompt: A pool keeps its resting rockets in a TArray and lends from the end with Pop. Why from the end?
choices: Pop is the only way to read a TArray
Taking the last element moves nothing else, so lending takes the same time however many rockets rest
The first element is always invalid
It makes the rockets spawn faster
recall.explanation: Removing from the end of an array shifts no other element, which gives the same constant-time take and return that a free list gives.

recall.prompt: A rocket comes back to the rack twice without being lent in between, and the rack adds it to the resting list both times. What goes wrong?
choices: Nothing, the second return is ignored by the engine
The rack later lends the same rocket to two users at once
recall.explanation: A rocket listed twice is handed out twice. A pool takes back only what it lent and has not yet taken back.

scenarios.prompt: Hit effects (decal plus sound plus spark actor) spawn dozens of times per second in a firefight, and Unreal Insights shows spawn cost spikes. Which pattern?
